Arranges components in the 2D space within a given boundary.

Useful for machines that can only cut straight edges, such as guillotines, knifes, table saws, shears, or other straight cutting tools. The 2D Rectangular solver uses a component's length and width to create a bounding rectangular around the component, which is then used to place the component on the envelope. You can also arrange non-rectangular components.
Arranges components in 2D space. Best suited for rectangular components.

The 3D solver creates a bounding box around each object and then uses the volume of the bounding box to fill up the available space. You define the available space by selecting a plane and then specifying length, height, and width dimensions.
Arranges components in 3D can be useful to see if the objects can fit within a given volume, such as a packaging box for example.
Arranges components in 3D space within a given volume.

Allows the arranging of components inside other components if empty space is available, making efficient use of the space on the envelope.
When deselected, each component is arranged on its own space in the envelope. You can deselect this option if for example there are limitations on your machine tool that make it difficult to cut the profile of components that are arranged inside other components.

Arranges components onto separate envelopes based on their physical material.
Envelopes with identical materials are placed along the X axis. Envelopes with different materials are placed along the Y axis.
If you change the material of any components, you can re-compute the arrangement by selecting Solid tab > Modify group > Compute All.
Note: When arranging by material, the Limit Envelope option applies to each material. For example, If you have two materials and you limit to one envelope then the result is two envelopes, one for each material.

Use Block From Object Mode to highlight objects in the browser, timeline, and configuration table to make it easier to create rules in context.
  • In the Toolbox, click Block From Object.
  • Click a highlighted object.
  • In the flyout, click the Getter or Setter blocks for the object to add to the rules canvas.
Tip: Use Block From Object Mode to save time finding exactly the Getter or Setter block you need for specific configured aspects by clicking on them direct.

Use the Getter block to reference configured aspect values in conditional statements.

The Getter block fetches the value of an aspect to define a condition in a rule.
  • Drag the block into the rules canvas.
  • Connect it to the if or else if portion of a Logic block.
  • Select the Category.
  • Select the Aspect.
  • Select the Operator.
  • Enter the relevant Value to fetch.
For example:
  • If a cabinet's Material is Wood
  • Then set Thickness to 20mm
  • Else if a cabinet's Material is Particle Board
  • Then set Thickness to 16mm
Tip: When the Value field is a dropdown, you can select multiple items.

Use the Logic block to create conditional logic within a rule.

For example:
  • If a cabinet's Height is less than 300mm
  • Then suppress the Shelf component
  • Else (otherwise) unsuppress the Shelf component
Use the Mutator to change the format of the logic block to suit your needs.
  • Click the Settings button in the upper left corner of the block.
  • In the flyout, drag the else or else if blocks from the left and connect them to the if block on the right.
Examples of logical formats:
  • if, else (default)
  • if, else if, else
  • if

Use the Rule block to create and manage rules that limit or drive configured aspects across a set of configurations.
  • The Rule block contains all the individual functions that define a rule.
  • Connect blocks like the Logic, Getter, and Setter to a Rule block to define the rule.
  • Click the State Toggle to turn the rule On or Off.
  • The Status tells you whether the rule is inactive, active, has pending changes, is running, or contains warnings or errors.
  • Blocks outside a Rule block are automatically disabled. They do not generate code or affect configurations.
Tip: While you can author all logical rules within a single Rule block, author multiple separate rules to make troubleshooting easier if something goes wrong.

Use the Setter block to limit or drive configured aspect values in configurations.

The Setter block defines the valid values of an aspect when the conditions of a rule are met.
  • Drag the block into the rules canvas.
  • Connect it directly to a Rule block or to a then portion of a Logic block.
  • Select the Category.
  • Select the Aspect.
  • Select the Operator.
  • Enter the relevant Value to fetch.
For example:
  • If a cabinet's Material is Wood
  • Then set Appearance to Walnut, Beech, or Oak
  • Else if a cabinet's Material is Particle Board
  • Then set Appearance to Blue, Green, or Yellow
Tip: You don't always need a Getter. Use a Setter by itself when you want to assign valid values to a configured aspect under all conditions.

The Toolbox on the left side organizes blocks into categories related to Fusion Configurations. Each category contains blocks you can use to create logical rules that limit or drive values in your configurations.
  • Click or drag a block from any category in the Toolbox to place it in the rules canvas.
  • Click Block From Object to quickly find the blocks you need in context.
The Rules category contains the Rule and Comment blocks.

The Logic category contains the Logic, And/Or, Not, and generic Getter and Setter blocks.

All other categories contain a Getter and Setter block, pre-filled with the selected category.
